title: The agent used my token somewhere else
goal: {{mark}}'s token was issued for {{vocab.billing}}. An attacker wants to use it at {{vocab.gateway}} to read {{vocab.assets}}.
obstacle: The token is genuine: real signature, real issuer, real user. Nothing about it looks forged.
control: Audience binding: the server accepts a token only if its aud names that server. The MCP authorization page says servers MUST validate that tokens were issued for them; RFC 8707 has the authorization server restrict tokens to the named resource.
say: A good token for one place must be worthless at every other place.

steps.title: {{mark}}'s token is issued for {{vocab.billing}}
steps.tell: The authorization server issues a genuine token. Read the decoded claims: aud names {{vocab.billing}}, not {{vocab.gateway}}.
steps.say: This token is real and it is {{mark}}'s. It was made for {{vocab.billing}}.
steps.why: The audience is the token's address label. Everything else can be perfect and it is still the wrong address.

steps.title: The attacker presents it at {{vocab.gateway}}
steps.tell: The same token arrives at a different server. Watch the request trail: the authorization header is redacted and the decoded claims are shown instead.
steps.why: Passing a token to a server it was not issued for is the token passthrough pattern the MCP security page tells servers to refuse.

steps.title: Does the server look at aud?
steps.tell: Ungoverned: signature and issuer check out, so the server accepts it. The flaw is the missing audience check, not a forged token.
steps.say: Signature valid is not the same as meant for me.
steps.why: Most of the checks pass. Only one question matters here.

blocked.tell: Governed: the server compares aud with its own identifier and answers 401 invalid_token. The refusal names the control and the flag that turned it on.
blocked.say: The server asked whether the token was meant for it. It was not.

steps.title: What the attacker gets
steps.tell: Ungoverned: {{mark}}'s account list comes back, highlighted as the attacker's gain.
steps.say: No hacking, only a token in the wrong place.
steps.why: The damage is whatever the gateway lets any valid token do.

blocked.tell: Governed: nothing comes back. There is no gain panel, only the refusal.

steps.title: Prove the control is the reason
steps.tell: On the governed side, tick the toggle that turns audience binding off and launch again. The attack succeeds. Turn it back on and it fails again.
steps.say: I can switch the one control off and the attack works. That is the proof.
steps.why: A claim that a control stops an attack means little until removing it brings the attack back.

proof.happy: The decoded token: aud is {{vocab.billing}}, yet the gateway returned data.
proof.blocked: 401 invalid_token naming audience binding, with flag audience_binding ON; flip it OFF and the same attack succeeds.
